routes.description: Justify Hirsi Ali's Christian turn by connecting transformative personal experience and chosen faith with Christianity's moral character, inherited institutions, and claimed necessity for Western civilizational renewal.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that her experience provides a legitimate personal basis for conversion, that Christianity offers a defensible affirmative moral framework, and that renewing it answers a consequential institutional and ideological vacuum not adequately filled by secular alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect personal transformation, Christian truth commitments, and civilizational need into a sufficient justification for Hirsi Ali's Christian turn.

centralBridges.description: Explain how the crisis, prayer, perceived encounter with a higher reality, and recovery can rationally support a personal commitment to Christianity.
Establish that Christianity's central teachings and exemplar provide an affirmative moral vision materially distinct from the rival religious ideology under discussion.
Show that the removal of Christian formation created an institutional moral vacuum and that Christian renewal can supply what secular alternatives have not organized or transmitted.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why inherited faith, education, organization, and active counter-messaging are needed to transmit the proposed moral framework across generations.
Require criticism of Christian institutions to identify a viable replacement capable of moral formation and resistance to destructive ideological recruitment.

routes.description: Reject the proposed justification by separating psychological or social benefits from the truth of Christianity's supernatural claims, challenging its asserted moral authority, and identifying rational secular resources for morality and ideological resistance.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that personal recovery and civilizational usefulness do not demonstrate Christian truth, that Christianity's doctrines or institutions cannot simply be assumed morally authoritative, and that rational secular alternatives defeat the claim of religious necessity.

motionBridge.description: Require the Christian turn to satisfy a truth test independent of consolation, meaning, institutional utility, or desirable social consequences.

centralBridges.description: Identify Christianity's definite supernatural commitments and require evidence proportionate to their universe-defining factual significance.
Test whether Christian doctrines and institutions merit the moral authority assigned to them rather than deriving that authority from their religious status.
Show that humanism, rational inquiry, and moral philosophy can supply standards of judgment without adding supernatural beliefs.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the consoling, motivational, or organizational effects of faith from evidence that its existential propositions are true.
Explain how enlightened rationality can oppose dangerous ideology without using a less extreme religious commitment as a protective instrument.

sections.title: Personal experience and conversion
sections.rationale: The motion expressly places Hirsi Ali's crisis, prayer, recovery, and chosen commitment against the objection that a transformative experience alone cannot establish a particular religion.

sections.title: Supernatural truth and practical benefit
sections.rationale: The central truth-test clash asks whether meaning, consolation, and social usefulness can justify belief when Christianity also makes definite factual claims about supernatural reality.

sections.title: Christian moral character and religious distinction
sections.rationale: The civilizational case depends on Christianity's moral content and its claimed distinction from Islam, while the opposing route contests both its doctrines and the asserted categorical difference.

sections.title: Moral formation and secular alternatives
sections.rationale: The alleged moral vacuum must be tested against secular humanism and moral philosophy, including whether either religious or secular institutions can transmit an effective framework to younger generations.

sections.title: Civilizational defense and ideological resistance
sections.rationale: The concluding burden concerns whether renewed Christian belief is needed to resist Islamist recruitment and defend Western inheritance or whether rationality can answer the threat without religion.

routes.description: Argue that consciousness is metaphysically fundamental and that religious and moral experience, purposive agency, and the universe's intelligible regularity jointly make best sense if reality has a conscious, intelligent, and purposive divine ground.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if mind-first theism supplies a coherent common explanation of the disputed phenomena and the cumulative connection from those phenomena to a divine ground is stronger than treating each as an unexplained or naturally generated appearance.

motionBridge.description: Establish that a God-centered mind-first reality provides the best unified account of consciousness, religious and moral experience, free agency, and cosmic intelligibility.

centralBridges.description: Establish that conscious experience cannot be reduced to or identified with physical processes and is more plausibly fundamental than matter.
Connect fundamental consciousness to a universal, intelligent, purposive ground capable of explaining the existence and character of the universe.
Show that religious and moral experiences are reasonably interpreted as awareness of transcendent mind and objective obligation rather than merely adaptive projection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend the coherence of mentality that is not dependent on an ordinary brain, supporting the intelligibility of a divine mind and personal survival.
Relate purposive freedom and the universe's regularities to an intentional origin rather than blind necessity.

routes.description: Argue that acknowledged mysteries about consciousness, experience, morality, freedom, and natural regularity do not uniquely support God because naturalistic accounts remain available and adding a divine mind does not close the explanatory gaps.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the phenomena remain reasonably compatible with agnostic naturalism, their theistic interpretations are underdetermined, and invoking God provides no necessary or independently supported explanatory advantage.

motionBridge.description: Establish that the shared phenomena admit non-theistic interpretations and therefore do not make a God-centered reality the best-supported conclusion.

centralBridges.description: Show that an unresolved brain-consciousness gap warrants uncertainty rather than an inference to idealism, bodiless mind, or God.
Show that labeling reality mental or invoking divine consciousness does not explain finite persons, objective reality, or the origin of consciousness.
Account for religious and moral experience through evolved psychological and social capacities without positing transcendent objects or objective divine commands.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish logical conceivability from evidential reasonableness when assessing brain-independent mentality and reported near-death experiences.
Defend meaningful compatibilist freedom and show that wonder at existence and natural regularity remains open to divergent metaphysical interpretations.

sections.title: Consciousness and the relation between mind and matter
sections.rationale: This issue contains the foundational clash over the epistemic primacy of experience, the brain-consciousness explanatory gap, material reduction, idealism, and whether consciousness should be treated as fundamental.

sections.title: Bodiless mind, personal identity, and the divine ground
sections.rationale: The coherence and evidential support for brain-independent mentality bear directly on personal survival and on whether a conscious, purposive ground of the universe is a genuine explanation rather than an unsupported addition.

sections.title: Religious experience and evolutionary explanation
sections.rationale: The competing interpretations of transformative and cross-cultural religious experience test whether such experience supplies contact with transcendent mind or can be explained through evolved agency detection, imagination, and cultural variation.

sections.title: Moral experience and objective obligation
sections.rationale: The status of obligations that appear to bind independently of desire determines whether moral experience supports an objective God-connected order or is adequately understood as an evolution-produced social disposition.

sections.title: Freedom, purpose, and the interpretation of cosmic mystery
sections.rationale: The dispute over compatibilist agency, intentional creation, natural regularities, and shared wonder tests whether purposive theism unifies these phenomena or whether they remain compatible with agnostic naturalism and multiple paradigms.

routes.description: Establish the nature and commands of God as a unified foundation for objective moral value and obligation, then show that this account explains the relevant moral phenomena with fewer or less serious foundational difficulties than godless normative realism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if divine nature supplies a nonarbitrary standard of goodness, divine authority constitutes universally applicable duties, and the resulting account retains a comparative explanatory advantage over irreducible godless normativity.

motionBridge.description: Connect God's necessarily good nature and authoritative commands to a comparatively adequate account of both objective moral values and objective duties.

centralBridges.description: Explain why God's essential nature can constitute the paradigm of moral goodness without appealing to an independent moral standard.
Explain how commands consistent with God's nature generate genuine obligations while allowing derivative principles and morally relevant circumstances to govern particular cases.
Show that the rival account's irreducible moral entities and natural-to-moral relations lack sufficient metaphysical or explanatory support.
Preserve responsible agency and moral knowledge under the theistic account while identifying whether the rival naturalistic setting can support both.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for how divine moral requirements bind agents who do not explicitly identify God as their source, including difficult cases of impaired moral understanding.
Explain the role of general divine commands in responsibility, recognition of wrongdoing, and accountability despite anticipated disobedience.

routes.description: Establish irreducible normative facts and morally relevant nondivine features as sufficient grounds for objective value and obligation, then show that appeals to God neither uniquely explain those facts nor avoid comparable explanatory stopping points.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if godless normative realism accounts for objective goodness, duties, agency, and moral knowledge while the proposed theistic foundation proves unnecessary or rests on equally basic normative assumptions.

motionBridge.description: Connect irreducible moral facts and morally relevant features of situations to a complete, nondivine account of objective moral values and duties.

centralBridges.description: Explain how intrinsic values and irreducible normative relations can be basic features of reality and can ground obligations without divine commands.
Show that suffering, promises, capacities, and other morally relevant facts can generate duties without requiring an additional divine order.
Establish that theistic grounding also terminates in normative assumptions or unexplained relations, preventing obscurity objections from yielding a comparative advantage.
Provide a godless account compatible with responsible mental causation and justified confidence in evolved cognitive and moral faculties.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether commands can bind agents who do not apprehend their source or authority and whether the theory treats impaired agents consistently.
Determine whether divine commands add a necessary normative function beyond communicating existing good and evil, especially when disobedience is anticipated.

sections.title: Ultimate Ground of Moral Value
sections.rationale: The competing accounts must identify what makes goodness and badness objective: God's essential nature or irreducible normative features. This issue also tests whether either proposed standard imports an unexplained normative premise.

sections.title: Constitution and Scope of Objective Duty
sections.rationale: The motion expressly includes duties, making the dispute between authoritative divine commands and obligations generated by morally relevant nondivine facts a principal burden for both sides.

sections.title: Metaphysical Relations and Explanatory Ultimates
sections.rationale: Both routes depend on foundational relations linking their proposed grounds to moral facts. The comparative burden includes ontology, causal or constitutive intelligibility, theoretical economy, and the legitimacy of explanatory stopping points.

sections.title: Universality, Accountability, and the Purpose of Commands
sections.rationale: An account of duty must explain who is bound, how authority reaches unaware or impaired agents, why commands are needed, and how wrongdoing and accountability arise when commands are violated.

sections.title: Moral Agency and Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: Objective duties require agents capable of responsible action, while objective moral claims require defensible epistemic access. The rival accounts therefore must support freedom, mental efficacy, and reliable moral cognition.

routes.description: Establish that evolutionary mechanisms do not entail unguidedness or exclude divine intention, then argue that naturalism combined with evolution creates an internal epistemic problem concerning trust in cognition.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the compatibility distinction survives evidential objections and if the account of selection, mental content, and conditional cognitive reliability supports the claimed self-defeat of naturalism plus evolution.

motionBridge.description: Connect the compatibility of theistic guidance with evolutionary science to the claim that the deeper epistemic conflict instead concerns naturalism plus evolution.

centralBridges.description: Show that evolutionary concepts such as random mutation and contingency do not themselves entail metaphysical unguidedness or the denial of design.
Establish that selection for adaptive neurophysiology and behavior does not by itself ensure the truth of associated propositional content.
Explain why low conditional confidence in cognitive reliability would generate an undefeated defeater extending to belief in naturalism and evolution themselves.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why scientific counterevidence or the bare availability of unguided explanations need not by itself eliminate rational warrant for theistic belief.
Distinguish the methods used in scientific investigation from a metaphysical commitment that no divine cause exists.

routes.description: Grant the logical possibility of intervention while denying that compatibility supplies evidential support, then provide an evolutionary and scientific account of truth-tracking cognition that blocks the self-defeat argument.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if logical compatibility is separated from warranted explanation and if naturalistic evolution, cultural representation, and corrective inquiry can account for sufficiently reliable cognition without a divine guarantee.

motionBridge.description: Connect the evidential adequacy of naturalistic explanation with a non-self-defeating account of evolved and scientifically corrected cognition.

centralBridges.description: Show that an intelligent cause remaining logically possible does not supply evidence that evolutionary outcomes were intelligently guided.
Explain how adaptive cognitive systems can depend causally on tracking relevant features of the world and eliminating recurrent errors.
Account for increasing reliability through language, representation, measurement, engineering, and iterative scientific correction.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify the role of naturalistic inquiry in testing design claims and comparing them with explanations grounded in observable processes.
Provide a natural account of how religious beliefs can arise and persist without treating their prevalence as evidence of their truth.

routes.description: Establish that the precise and predictive applicability of independently developed mathematics is a genuine explanatory datum, remains contingent under naturalism, and is expected if a divine mind intentionally gives the physical world mathematical structure.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by preserving the surprising applicability datum against practical-development, approximation, and selection-effect objections, then showing that intentional divine construction supplies a deeper comparative explanation than naturalistic necessity.

motionBridge.description: Connect the surprising applicability of mathematics to an intentional divine ordering of creation and show why that connection supports theism better than naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Establish that mathematics developed by a priori standards nevertheless describes and predicts physical phenomena with accuracy that calls for explanation.
Show that provisional theories, approximate truth, non-instantiable mathematical structures, and unsuccessful applications do not dissolve the relevant explanatory datum.
Explain how divine conception and intentional creation can produce a world structured according to mathematics under either realist or anti-realist mathematical ontology.

Maintain that a nonexistent, chaotic, or mathematically inaccessible physical reality is metaphysically possible, so mathematical order cannot be explained merely by postulated naturalistic necessity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify the role of mathematical fruitfulness and richness in supporting sufficient independence from anticipated empirical application.
Distinguish an explanatory appeal to divine free choice from a bare restatement that mathematical structure or applicability is necessary.

routes.description: Challenge whether mathematical applicability is as independent, accurate, and selectively successful as alleged, then provide a naturalistic modal account on which mathematically formulable laws and boundary conditions are necessary rather than an unexplained coincidence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by undermining the claimed need for a distinctively theistic explanation or by showing that an independently motivated naturalistic necessity account explains the datum while divine freedom introduces an equivalent or deeper explanatory stopping point.

motionBridge.description: Show that naturalism can accommodate mathematical applicability without brute coincidence and that theism supplies no superior comparative explanation.

centralBridges.description: Contest the alleged unexpectedness of applicability by examining problem-driven mathematical development, false yet predictive theories, discarded solutions, and failed predictions.
Require a coherent account of how approximate, structurally inaccurate, or non-instantiable mathematics relates to the physical world before its success supports a metaphysical inference.
Derive mathematical applicability from a naturalistic cosmology whose laws and boundary conditions necessarily admit mathematical formulation.
Determine whether God could create a world lacking mathematical applicability and show how either necessity or brute divine choice affects the claimed explanatory advantage.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate truth-directed mathematical problem solving from aesthetic motivation without assuming that scientific utility directly drives mathematical research.
Frame modal necessity as part of an independently developed total metaphysical theory assessed through explanatory scope and economy.

sections.title: Unexpectedness and the Development of Mathematics
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether mathematics is sufficiently independent of physical inquiry, yet sufficiently accurate in application, to generate the initial explanatory burden on which the comparative argument depends.

sections.title: Truth, Approximation, and Physical Structure
sections.rationale: The relation between successful mathematical theories and actual physical structure matters because predictive accuracy can support the motion only if provisional or false theories still instantiate the relevant explanatory phenomenon.

sections.title: Instantiation and Nonphysical Mathematical Resources
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether physical structural instantiation exhausts the applicability datum or whether indispensable non-instantiable resources create an additional burden for both theistic and naturalistic explanations.

sections.title: Failed Applications and Selection Effects
sections.rationale: The balance between striking successes and numerous discarded solutions or failed predictions determines whether observed applicability is genuinely anomalous or partly produced by selective attention.

sections.title: Naturalistic Necessity and Modal Contingency
sections.rationale: This is a principal motion-level clash because the naturalistic rival depends on necessary mathematical order, while the theistic route depends on that order being contingent and intentionally selected.

sections.title: Divine Freedom and Explanatory Depth
sections.rationale: The dispute over necessary structure, free divine choice, brute stopping points, and independent theoretical motivation determines whether either worldview provides the deeper comparative explanation required by the motion.

routes.description: Establish objective moral facts by identifying attitude-independent moral truths, eliminating leading anti-realist interpretations of ordinary moral claims, and defending intellectual appearances as prima facie grounds for realist conclusions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if at least some moral propositions are justified as true independently of attitudes, rival semantic accounts fail to explain the relevant discourse, and ethical intuitions can legitimately support that conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Show that at least some justified moral truths retain their validity independently of individual or collective attitudes.

centralBridges.description: Reject global error theory, stance-dependent truth conditions, and non-cognitivist treatment as adequate accounts of the relevant moral judgments.
Establish that noninferential intellectual appearances receive prima facie epistemic weight and can ground reasoning toward realism.
Identify contexts in which moral assertions have propositionally structured, truth-apt content that cannot be reduced to expressive or attitude-reporting functions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how familiar first-order judgments can support realism without requiring ordinary speakers to begin with an explicit metaethical theory.
Clarify the distinctive practical authority claimed for objective moral reasons relative to preference-dependent considerations.

routes.description: Resist the inference to objective moral facts by denying that ordinary discourse or intuitive appearances determine realist commitments, developing a contextual quietist alternative, and challenging the epistemic and metaphilosophical assumptions of the realist argument.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the realist elimination is non-exhaustive, ordinary moral language remains meaningful without determinate realist content, and intuitive appearances lack sufficient shared or theory-neutral force to establish stance-independent facts.

motionBridge.description: Show that moral practice and discourse need not commit speakers to stance-independent moral facts and do not establish realism.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate that contextual, quietist, or indeterminate uses of moral language escape the realist taxonomy of anti-realist alternatives.
Show that realist appearances are disputed, interpretation-dependent, or shaped by pragmatic, cultural, linguistic, and philosophical conditions.
Account for meaningful moral communication through variable use and context without assigning uniform realist or anti-realist semantics.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Challenge attempts to infer a determinate folk metaethics from surveys or philosophically trained responses.
Explain why practical importance or motivation need not depend on stance-independent reasons or facts.

sections.title: Objective moral truth and the anti-realist alternatives
sections.rationale: This issue contains the motion-level dispute over attitude-independent truth and whether error theory, stance dependence, and non-cognitivism exhaust the alternatives to realism.

sections.title: Moral language, contextual use, and quietism
sections.rationale: The semantic clash determines whether ordinary assertions encode stable realist propositions or can remain meaningful through context-sensitive uses without determinate metaethical commitments.

sections.title: Intuition, intellectual appearances, and philosophical method
sections.rationale: Ethical intuitionism depends on the epistemic standing of pre-analytic appearances, while the opposing route challenges their interpretation, reliability, generality, and methodological role.

sections.title: Common sense, empirical evidence, and folk metaethics
sections.rationale: Claims about common sense affect the dialectical starting point, making the determinacy of ordinary commitments and the methods used to measure them materially burden-relevant.

sections.title: Normative authority, motivation, and practical significance
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether objectivity supplies distinctive authority or motivation and whether practical consequences can illuminate the difference between realist and preference-based morality.

routes.description: Establish that a beginningless temporal series is metaphysically impossible because it would instantiate an actual infinite and would require an actual infinite to be formed or traversed by successive addition.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the actual-infinity and successive-addition arguments withstand the principal modal, temporal-symmetry, cardinality, quantifier, and explanatory objections and thereby provide adequate philosophical support for the claim that the universe began to exist.

motionBridge.description: Show that the defended impossibility of a beginningless temporal series adequately supports the Kalam claim that the universe began to exist.

centralBridges.description: Justify the inference from Hilbert-style and related consequences to the metaphysical impossibility of a concretely instantiated actual infinite.
Provide a principled account of why a beginningless past would be actually infinite while an endless future may remain only potentially infinite.
Defend the claim that successive addition cannot form or traverse an actual infinite temporal series despite reaching each finite member.
Show that reverse-countdown, Grim Reaper, or causal-finitist reasoning identifies a genuine impossibility in a beginningless past.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend the every-versus-all distinction as applicable to endless counting and traversal rather than merely identifying an abstractly invalid inference form.
Explain why a beginningless countdown cannot adequately account for completion at one temporal point rather than another.

routes.description: Show that the actual-infinity and successive-addition arguments do not establish the metaphysical impossibility of a beginningless past, without undertaking the further burden of proving that the past is beginningless.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the disputed arguments leave a beginningless temporal series coherent or insufficiently excluded because their crucial inferences rely on counterintuitiveness, an undefended past-future asymmetry, equivocation about infinite completion, or inadequate paradox and explanation premises.

motionBridge.description: Show that dismantling one or more indispensable infinity-based inferences prevents them from providing adequate support for the Kalam beginning claim.

centralBridges.description: Show that strange properties of infinite collections do not establish metaphysical impossibility without contradiction or an independently defended modal principle.
Show that excluding a beginningless past while permitting an endless future requires a temporal symmetry breaker that the proposed tensed account does not adequately supply.
Distinguish encountering every finite member from reaching a terminal infinite ordinal and test whether the successive-addition argument equivocates between these claims.
Challenge the sufficiency, explanation, or causal assumptions needed for reverse-countdown, Grim Reaper, and related arguments to exclude a beginningless past.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Maintain the distinction between showing that the beginning arguments are inadequate and positively establishing that the universe had no beginning.
Require a concrete countermodel or case-specific demonstration before treating the alleged every-to-all inference as fallacious in the relevant infinite process.

sections.title: Do actual-infinity scenarios establish metaphysical impossibility?
sections.rationale: The actual-infinity argument depends on moving from Hilbert-style and related consequences to a modal conclusion about concrete temporal reality, making the warrant for that inference a primary burden issue.

sections.title: Can the past and future be treated asymmetrically?
sections.rationale: The case must explain why a beginningless past is an actual infinite while an endless future is merely potential, and whether tensed time or prior instantiation supplies the required principled difference.

sections.title: Can successive addition yield or traverse an infinite series?
sections.rationale: This is one of the two arguments expressly named in the motion and turns on whether an endless process involving every finite member constitutes an actual infinite despite having no terminal completion stage.

sections.title: Does the every-versus-all distinction resolve the counting dispute?
sections.rationale: The principal clash over successive addition depends on quantifier scope and simple-future versus future-perfect claims, so the applicability of the alleged inference error requires separate scrutiny.

sections.title: Do countdown and causal paradoxes exclude a beginningless past?
sections.rationale: Reverse countdowns, Grim Reapers, causal finitism, and related formulations provide alternative support whose force depends on disputed sufficiency, symmetry, causal, and explanatory principles.

routes.description: Establish that theism has a defensible prior and that fine-tuning, consciousness, ordered complexity, and observer existence jointly favor a limitless, knowledgeable, and morally perfect creator over relevant alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cumulative observations raise the probability of the specified being enough to warrant belief, with an adequate account of why the evidence points beyond an unspecified designer to the all-knowing, all-powerful, morally perfect being in the motion.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative evidential comparison to rationally warranted belief in the all-knowing, all-powerful, morally perfect being specified by the motion.

centralBridges.description: Establish a non-negligible prior for theism through simplicity, fundamentality, and the absence of arbitrary limits.
Show that observations can support theism through likelihood comparisons when assessed together with priors and cumulative evidence.
Show that life-permitting constants and complexity-generating laws are substantially more expected under purposive creation than under agentless alternatives.
Show that conscious lives and observer existence are more expected if a morally perfect, unconstrained creator has reason to create valuable lives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why observer selection, a single observed universe, or unknown alternative constants need not eliminate the evidential force attributed to fine-tuning.
Account for the universe's scale, hostility, development, and divine nonmanifestation insofar as they bear on its fit with purposive creation.

routes.description: Establish that the available observations do not discriminate the specified deity from natural, selection-based, or rival intentional explanations and therefore do not supply sufficient warrant for belief in an omnimax, morally perfect being.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative's likelihood claims lack adequate priors, comparison classes, causal discrimination, or an attribute-level bridge, or if features such as hiddenness and suffering materially undermine the prediction that this morally perfect being would produce the observed world.

motionBridge.description: Show that the evidence presented does not warrant belief in the all-knowing, all-powerful, morally perfect being named by the motion.

centralBridges.description: Require evidence to discriminate the proposed deity from competing explanations rather than merely remain consistent with intentional creation.
Show that conditional likelihood alone does not identify the actual cause without defensible priors, alternatives, and background causal information.
Test whether observer selection, unknown parameter possibilities, and the single-universe setting block the inference from life-permitting conditions to design.
Require a justified transition from evidence for possible agency or power to maximal knowledge, maximal power, and moral perfection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Examine whether moral perfection and self-sufficiency actually predict the creation of conscious, imperfect beings.
Assess whether hiddenness, unreliable supernatural expectations, suffering, and cosmic hostility fit the proposed morally perfect creator.

sections.title: Evidential Standards and Bayesian Support
sections.rationale: This issue governs when comparative likelihood, prior probability, and cumulative observations count as evidence rather than mere compatibility, determining how every substantive argument connects to warranted belief.

sections.title: Theistic Prior and the Omnimax Attribute Bridge
sections.rationale: The motion concerns a specifically all-knowing, all-powerful, morally perfect being, so the case must address both the prior plausibility of theism and the transition from a possible designer to those maximal attributes.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Design, and Observer Selection
sections.rationale: Life-permitting constants and ordered complexity form the most sustained evidential clash, encompassing design analogies, comparison classes, possible parameter values, anthropic selection, and rival explanations.

sections.title: Consciousness, Observer Existence, and Divine Motivation
sections.rationale: The predicted existence of conscious people depends on both their comparative probability under alternative worldviews and whether a morally perfect, unconstrained being would have reason to create them.

sections.title: Divine Hiddenness and the Observed World's Fit
sections.rationale: Hiddenness, suffering, cosmic hostility, and unreliable supernatural expectations bear directly on whether the observed world is expected under a morally perfect creator and therefore on the motion-level inference.

routes.description: Establish that the universe’s origin and order, objective morality, evidence concerning Jesus, and religious experience cumulatively favor Christian theism, while showing that naturalistic evidence from evolution, suffering, and hiddenness does not reverse that comparison.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its independent and mutually reinforcing considerations warrant a transcendent personal God and connect that conclusion to Christian theism, with adequate answers to the principal naturalistic likelihood arguments.

motionBridge.description: The total evidence is more expected under Christian theism than under agnostic naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Cosmic beginning and life-permitting order require support for a transcendent personal creator and intelligent design.
Objective moral values and duties require an adequate foundation in God rather than an exclusively naturalistic ontology.
The historical case for Jesus’s resurrection must support divine action and authenticate distinctively Christian revelation.
Evolution, pain, tragedy, and hiddenness must be reconciled with Christian theism sufficiently to preserve the cumulative comparison.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The cause of a temporally finite universe must be connected defensibly to timelessness, immateriality, power, and personal agency.
Religious experience must provide defeasible warrant that coheres with the route’s independent arguments.

routes.description: Show cumulatively that major features of minds, life, suffering, moral behavior, and religious uncertainty are more probable under agnostic naturalism, while limiting the claimed force of cosmological, moral, resurrection, and experiential arguments for Christian theism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the comparative likelihood of the total evidence favors agnostic naturalism, or if the pro considerations remain too underdetermined to outweigh the naturalistic evidence without requiring a conclusive proof of naturalism.

motionBridge.description: The total evidence is more expected under agnostic naturalism than under Christian theism.

centralBridges.description: Each material fact must be compared by its relative probability under the rival worldviews and then incorporated cumulatively.
Evolution, mind-brain dependence, and the biological distribution of pain and pleasure must receive stronger expectations under naturalism.
Apparently uncompensated tragedy, absent divine comfort, and unclear religious revelation must count as evidence against Christian theism.
Cosmological, moral, resurrection, and experiential considerations must fail to supply a sufficient comparative advantage for Christian theism.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Objective moral truths and value must admit accounts that do not depend on grounding them in God’s nature.
Appeals to unknown goods, compensation, or compatibility must address comparative probability rather than mere logical consistency.

sections.title: Comparative probability and the cumulative burden
sections.rationale: Defines how multiple independent facts bear on the motion, including the distinction between showing evidence more likely on one worldview and conclusively proving that worldview.

sections.title: Cosmic origin, fine-tuning, and design
sections.rationale: Covers the universe’s beginning, causal explanation, inferred divine attributes, life-permitting conditions, and whether these facts favor personal design over naturalistic alternatives.

sections.title: Evolution, consciousness, and biological order
sections.rationale: Addresses evolutionary common descent, complex biological systems, mind-brain dependence, and pain-and-pleasure functions as competing evidence for design or naturalistic development.

sections.title: Morality, value, and human conduct
sections.rationale: Examines objective moral truth, possible divine and naturalistic grounds of value, moral disagreement, and the evidential significance of comparative moral behavior among believers.

sections.title: Jesus, revelation, and religious experience
sections.rationale: Tests the historical and inferential route from resurrection claims to divine authentication alongside experiential warrant, religious disagreement, and alternative interpretations.

sections.title: Suffering, divine comfort, and hiddenness
sections.rationale: Evaluates tragedy, biologically structured suffering, absent experiences of divine comfort, and proposed greater-good, doctrinal, compensatory, or epistemic explanations under the rival worldviews.

routes.description: Establish Christian theism as more reasonable than skeptical atheism through a cumulative case from cosmic origins, fine-tuning, objective morality, Jesus' resurrection, and direct religious experience, while addressing proposed defeaters.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the principal evidential strands jointly support a personal, morally perfect creator and the Christian identification of that creator more strongly than the skeptical alternatives undermine those inferences.

motionBridge.description: The combined evidence must make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: A beginning of the universe and an applicable causal principle must support a transcendent personal creator.
Life-permitting fine-tuning must favor intelligent design over necessity, chance, or selection-based alternatives.
Objective moral values and duties must require and receive an adequate foundation in God.
Resurrection evidence and religious experience must connect generic theism to the Christian-God hypothesis.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The evidential strands must be assessed cumulatively under a burden that also requires justification for skeptical atheism.
Objections from evil, hiddenness, religious diversity, and naturalistic epistemology must not defeat the cumulative inference.

routes.description: Show that the specific Christian-God hypothesis lacks sufficient evidential support because its main arguments rely on disputed premises, exceed their conclusions, face natural alternatives, and conflict with evil and hiddenness.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative evidence does not adequately distinguish Christian theism from rival explanations and the observed world supplies material counterevidence to the claimed divine attributes.

motionBridge.description: The evidence must fail to make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: Neither an absolute cosmic beginning nor a causal inference to an immaterial personal creator must be treated as established.
Fine-tuning and morality must admit alternatives that prevent their use as distinctive evidence for the Christian God.
Resurrection reports and religious experience must lack the reliability needed to distinguish Christianity from natural or rival religious accounts.
Evil, suffering, and sincere nonbelief must count against a perfectly good, omnipotent, relational God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Christian theism must bear an appropriately demanding burden as one specific supernatural hypothesis among incompatible alternatives.
Any limited anomaly or unexplained cause must not be extended beyond the evidence to the full divine attributes.

sections.title: Burden, Religious Diversity, and Epistemic Method
sections.rationale: This issue governs how the specific Christian hypothesis is compared with skeptical atheism, rival religions, experiential claims, rational intuition, and empirically grounded inquiry.

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
sections.rationale: This issue contains the principal inference from the universe's alleged beginning through causal premises to a timeless, immaterial, personal cause.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Design, and Alternative Explanations
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether life-permitting conditions favor intelligent design and whether that inference reaches the kind of God specified by the motion.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Divine Grounding
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether objective value and obligation exist, whether non-theistic accounts can ground them, and whether a divine lawgiver is required.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Religious Experience
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on the transition from generic theism to Christianity through historical claims about Jesus and purported immediate awareness of God.

sections.title: Evil, Suffering, and Divine Hiddenness
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether suffering and sincere nonbelief conflict with the claimed divine attributes and whether the proposed theistic purposes answer that conflict.
